title: Emerson's Nature
hookLine: his book Nature begins with going out alone under the stars

lines: AN ORIGINAL RELATION TO THE UNIVERSE.
cards: "Our age is retrospective." That's how it opens, a small book with a one-word title: Nature. Emerson's complaint is that his own time keeps looking backward, seeing God and the world through the eyes of people long dead.
Then he asks a question that sounds simple and isn't: "Why should not we also enjoy an original relation to the universe?" Not secondhand. Not inherited.
Your own. And when he turns, in the first chapter, to how you might get it, his answer isn't a church or a library. It's the night sky.

teach.h: LEAVE THE CHAMBER, NOT JUST SOCIETY.
teach.b: First, what solitude takes. Emerson begins: "To go into solitude, a man needs to retire as much from his chamber as from society." Leaving people isn't enough.
You also have to leave the room where you keep your books and your thoughts. Second, why the study doesn't count. "I am not solitary whilst I read and write, though nobody is with me."
Reading is company. Writing is a conversation. Third, his answer.

teach.h: IF A MAN WOULD BE ALONE, LOOK UP.
teach.b: "But if a man would be alone, let him look at the stars." The light from those worlds, he says, sets a little distance between you and the ordinary things you handle all day.

He even suggests the air might have been made clear for this reason, so that people would always have something vast in view. Fourth, what he does not say. He doesn't say leave your faith, or leave your people.
He says step outside, look up, and let something older than every book you own come to you directly.
That's the original relation he's after: not a new doctrine, a first-hand look.

teach.h: AN ORIGINAL RELATION TO THE UNIVERSE.
teach.b: Emerson had come through hard years, a death, a pulpit given up, and the book he wrote begins not with an argument but with a man stepping out of his study into the dark.
That walk is still short: a back step, a balcony, a window on the stairs.

how: Readers of Emerson's Nature sometimes take its opening literally, stepping outside at night without a book or a phone to look at the stars as a way of being alone.

games.why: "if a man would be alone, let him look at the stars." his study doesn't count, because reading and writing are company.

practice: If it's night and you can, step outside now and look up, with the phone left in your pocket; if it's daytime, or cloudy, or you can't get out, go to a window and find as much sky as you can, or close your eyes and bring back the last night sky you really saw.
No names of stars, no apps: just the dark, the points of light, and you.
